usage: the single most common partner; 날씨가 덥다 is the default frame for complaining about heat
the modifier form is 더운 (the final ㅂ drops and 우 appears), not 덥은
the mimetic 푹푹 찌다 ('to steam') intensifies it for a humid Korean summer
the noun 더위 ('the heat') comes from 덥다; 더위를 타다 means heat affects you badly
examples: the bare 요-form; note 덥다 turns into 더워요, never 덥어요
더운 directly modifies 여름; this is the noun-modifier shape
에어컨이 고장 나서 사무실이 너무 더워요.
The office is too hot because the air conditioner broke.
real-situation use with -아서 giving the cause
nuance: 덥다 is the ㅂ-irregular adjective for FELT air temperature being unpleasantly high — hot weather, a stuffy room, a sweaty body. The key English-speaker trap is that English 'hot' covers four different Korean words: use 덥다 ONLY for ambient air/weather. A hot object you touch is 뜨겁다 (뜨거운 커피, never 더운 커피), spicy food is 맵다, and pleasant warmth is 따뜻하다. Because it is ㅂ-irregular, the ㅂ becomes 우 before a vowel: 덥다 → 더워요(polite) → 더운(modifier) → 더우니까(reason) → 더워서. Beginners constantly write 덥어요 or 덥은 by treating it as regular — that is the number-one error. It is neutral in register and used by everyone; the related noun is 더위 ('the heat'), and people say 더위를 먹다 to mean 'suffer heatstroke.'

usage: the default collocation, exactly mirroring 날씨가 덥다 for heat
modifier form is 추운, never 춥은; the ㅂ becomes 우
the noun 추위 ('the cold') derives from 춥다, like 더위 from 덥다
cold enough to sting your hands
시리다 ('to sting from cold') pairs with bitter winter weather
examples: bare polite form; 춥다 → 추워요, never 춥어요
추운 modifies 겨울 in the noun-modifier shape
창문이 열려 있어서 방이 너무 추워요.
The room is too cold because the window is open.
nuance: 춥다 is the ㅂ-irregular adjective for ambient air being unpleasantly cold — winter, a chilly room, a draft. The crucial contrast for English speakers is 춥다 vs 차갑다: 춥다 is how the WEATHER/AIR feels to your whole body, while 차갑다 is how a cold OBJECT feels to your hand (차가운 물 'cold water', 차가운 손 'cold hands'). Never say 추운 물 — water is 차갑다. As a ㅂ-irregular it conjugates 춥다 → 추워요 → 추운 → 추우니까 → 추워서, so writing 춥어요 or 춥은 (the regular pattern) is the classic beginner slip. It is register-neutral and universal. The matching noun is 추위, and 추위를 타다 means 'to be cold-sensitive,' the exact mirror of 더위를 타다.

usage: modifier form 따뜻한; 따뜻하다 is a regular 하다-adjective, so 하 + ㄴ = 한
the figurative use for kindness, just like English 'a warm person'
the pleasant-spring-weather sense, opposite of the unpleasant 덥다
with -아지다 ('become'), often after a touching moment
examples: 따뜻한 modifies 봄; describes pleasant mild weather
할머니가 따뜻하게 안아 주셔서 마음이 놓였어요.
Grandmother hugged me warmly, so I felt at ease.
real-situation use with the adverb 따뜻하게 and a figurative 'warm' nuance
nuance: 따뜻하다 means pleasantly, comfortably warm and is overwhelmingly POSITIVE — that is what separates it from 덥다, which is the unpleasant 'too hot.' It stretches across three domains: weather (따뜻한 봄날), temperature of food/drink (따뜻한 국), and emotional warmth (따뜻한 사람, 따뜻한 말 'kind words'). The near-synonym 뜨겁다 is for things hot enough to burn, so 따뜻한 커피 is comfortably drinkable while 뜨거운 커피 is scalding — choosing wrong sounds odd. As a 하다-adjective it conjugates predictably: 따뜻하다 → 따뜻해요 (note 하 + 아 → 해), 따뜻한, 따뜻하게(adverb), 따뜻해서. The pitfall: learners write 따뜻하요 by forgetting that 하 + 여/아 contracts to 해. Register is neutral and the word is everywhere in everyday speech.

mistakes: Writing 따뜻하요 — every 하다-adjective contracts 하 + 아 into 해, so the polite form is 따뜻해요.
Using 따뜻하다 for very hot food/drink. Comfortably warm tea is 따뜻한 차; scalding coffee is 뜨거운 커피 (from 뜨겁다).
Treating it as a verb and asking 따뜻해요? to mean 'do you warm?' — it is a state adjective ('is warm'), so 따뜻해요? simply asks 'is it warm?'

usage: modifier 시원한; the prototypical pleasant-cool collocation
idiom for emotional relief OR a soup that settles the stomach
the broth tastes clean and refreshing
a uniquely Korean food praise — note it does NOT mean the soup is cold
examples: 시원한 modifies 물; here it is literal pleasant coolness
It's piping-hot broth, yet it's so refreshing.
real-situation paradox: a HOT soup can be 시원하다 because it clears the body — the key cultural nuance
nuance: 시원하다 is the positive counterpart to 차갑다/춥다: it means PLEASANTLY cool and, by extension, refreshing or relieving. Its famous quirk for English speakers is that 시원하다 ≠ 'cold': a hot spicy soup is praised as 시원하다 (시원한 국물) because it clears your sinuses and settles your stomach, and a hot spring or a good back-scratch is also 시원하다. So unlike 차갑다 (purely low temperature), 시원하다 is about the refreshing SENSATION. It also covers emotional relief — 속이 시원하다 'I feel relieved/it's off my chest.' As a 하다-adjective: 시원하다 → 시원해요 → 시원한 → 시원하게 → 시원해서. The trap is writing 시원하요 (must contract to 시원해요) and assuming it always means 'cold' — temperature-cold drinks are better 차갑다/차가운. Register is neutral and conversational.

usage: modifier form 밝은 (regular: stem 밝- + 은); the ㄹ is silent but written
the figurative 'sunny, upbeat' sense, very common in describing people
fixed expression for dawn; 날이 밝으면 = 'when day breaks'
for color tone, opposite of 어두운 색 ('dark color')
examples: regular polite form 밝아요 (밝- + 아요); the ㄱ links to the vowel
밝은 modifies 색; the color-tone meaning
그 친구는 항상 밝아서 같이 있으면 기분이 좋아요.
That friend is always cheerful, so I feel good around them.
nuance: 밝다 covers brightness of LIGHT (a sunlit room, a lit lamp), lightness of a COLOR (밝은 파랑 'light blue'), and figuratively a CHEERFUL personality (성격이 밝다). It is a regular adjective despite the ㄹㄱ cluster: 밝다 → 밝아요 (the 받침 keeps both consonants but the ㄱ pronounces as /k→g/), 밝은, 밝아서. A useful near-synonym is 환하다, which means brightly/glowingly lit and is more about a flood of light or a beaming smile (환한 미소), whereas 밝다 is the broad neutral word and the only one used for cheerful character or for clear eyesight/hearing (귀가 밝다 'sharp-eared'). Pitfall one: confusing the spelling with 밤 ('night') or 밥 ('rice') — 밝다 is bright. Pitfall two: pronouncing it; 밝다 sounds like [박따], and 밝아요 like [발가요], which trips learners up.

usage: modifier form 어두운, never 어둡은; 어둡다 is ㅂ-irregular so the ㅂ becomes 우
figurative use; a 어두운 표정 is a troubled, sad face
the color-tone sense, the direct opposite of 밝은 색
with -아지다 for the change at dusk
examples: ㅂ-irregular polite form 어두워요, not 어둡어요
어두운 modifies 골목 in the noun-modifier shape
전기가 나가서 집 안이 갑자기 어두워졌어요.
The power went out, so the house suddenly got dark.
nuance: 어둡다 is the exact opposite of 밝다 and, like 밝다, spans three layers: physical darkness (an unlit room, nighttime), dark COLOR tone (어두운 회색 'dark gray'), and a figurative GLOOMY mood or expression (표정이 어둡다, 분위기가 어둡다). Crucially it is ㅂ-IRREGULAR — 어둡다 → 어두워요 → 어두운 → 어두우니까 → 어두워서 — so the single most common beginner error is the regular-looking 어둡어요/어둡은. A near-synonym is 캄캄하다 ('pitch-dark'), which is far stronger: a room with no light at all is 캄캄하다, while 어둡다 is the general 'dark/dim.' One more nuance learners miss: 어둡다 can mean 'poorly informed' — 세상 물정에 어둡다 'naive about the world' or 길에 어둡다 'bad with directions,' mirroring how 밝다 means 'well-informed/sharp.' Register is neutral.

usage: modifier 시끄러운, never 시끄럽은; ㅂ-irregular changes ㅂ to 우
adverb 시끄럽게 + 하다; what a teacher tells noisy kids to stop doing
literally 'the ears are noisy,' a vivid complaint about loudness
blunt casual register; said to friends or family, not to elders
examples: ㅂ-irregular polite form 시끄러워요, not 시끄럽어요
시끄러운 modifies 음악 in the noun-modifier shape
옆집 공사 소리 때문에 너무 시끄러워서 잠을 못 잤어요.
It was so noisy from the neighbor's construction that I couldn't sleep.
nuance: 시끄럽다 means unpleasantly LOUD or noisy — places, sounds, machines, and people can all be 시끄럽다, and it is the direct opposite of 조용하다. It is ㅂ-IRREGULAR: 시끄럽다 → 시끄러워요 → 시끄러운 → 시끄러우니까 → 시끄러워서, so 시끄럽어요/시끄럽은 are the predictable beginner mistakes. Two register cautions: first, 시끄러워! barked at someone literally means 'shut up!' and is rude, so reserve it for very casual settings; politely you'd say 조금 시끄럽네요 or ask 조용히 해 주세요. Second, distinguish it from 떠들다, which is a VERB meaning 'to chatter/make a racket' (아이들이 떠들어요 'the kids are being rowdy') — 시끄럽다 describes the resulting state, 떠들다 the action. There is also a figurative 'a fuss/controversy is loud' use: 세상이 시끄럽다 'the world is in an uproar.'

usage: modifier 조용한 (하 + ㄴ); the go-to phrase for a peaceful spot
adverb 조용히 + 하다; 조용히 해! is the everyday 'be quiet!'
to have a quiet, reserved nature
figurative use for a calm, soft-spoken person
to pass by quietly / blow over
for an event that ends without fuss
examples: I study at a quiet cafe.
조용한 modifies 카페 in the noun-modifier shape
Since night fell, the neighborhood became very quiet.
nuance: 조용하다 is the opposite of 시끄럽다 and covers both a quiet PLACE/sound and a calm, reserved PERSONALITY (성격이 조용하다 = soft-spoken, low-key). (using 조용히), not 조용하게 — Koreans overwhelmingly use 조용히 here, so memorize it as a set phrase. The near-synonym 고요하다 is more literary/poetic and means a deep, serene stillness (고요한 밤 'a serene night'), whereas 조용하다 is the everyday neutral word you'd actually speak. Pitfall: writing 조용하요 instead of the contracted 조용해요, and reaching for 조용하게 when 조용히 is the natural adverb. Register is neutral and extremely common.

usage: modifier 넓은 (regular: 넓- + 은); the ㄼ cluster is kept in spelling
figurative: a 마음이 넓은 사람 is tolerant and forgiving
to have a wide social network
idiom — literally 'wide feet,' meaning 'knows lots of people'
for the breadth of a road/path, contrasted with 좁은 길
examples: regular polite form 넓어요; the ㅂ of the cluster links to the vowel
I took a walk in a spacious park.
넓은 modifies 공원 in the noun-modifier shape
이 집은 거실이 넓어서 가족이 모이기 좋아요.
This house has a spacious living room, so it's good for the family to gather.
nuance: 넓다 describes a wide AREA or surface — a room, a road, a field, a forehead — and is the opposite of 좁다. The essential contrast English speakers must learn is 넓다 vs 크다: 넓다 is two-dimensional spaciousness (floor area, breadth), while 크다 is overall bigness/size. A studio can be 작지만 넓다 ('small in size yet feels open'), and Koreans say 방이 넓다 for a roomy floor plan but 집이 크다 for a large house overall — mixing them sounds off. It is a regular adjective: 넓다 → 넓어요 (pronounced [널버요], the ㅂ of the ㄼ cluster surfaces), 넓은, 넓어서. Two famous idioms ride on it: 마음이 넓다 'broad-minded/generous' and 발이 넓다 'well-connected socially.' The pronunciation pitfall is that 넓다 is [널따] and 넓어요 is [널버요], not [넙어요]. Register is neutral and everyday.

usage: with 폭 ('width') for roads, rivers, fabric
the classic phrase for tight back-streets in old neighborhoods
examples: I walked carefully along the narrow path.
좁은 modifies 길 in the noun-modifier shape

The English-speaker pitfall mirrors 넓다: keep 좁다 (cramped/narrow in area) separate from 짧다 (short in LENGTH). A short pencil is 짧다, never 좁다; a narrow corridor is 좁다, never 짧다. Figuratively, 마음이 좁다 ('narrow-minded, petty') and 속이 좁다 ('small-hearted, easily offended') are the negative counterparts to 넓다's generous idioms. Register is neutral. what you wear in winter; opposite of 얇은 옷
with the noun 두께 ('thickness'), itself derived from 두껍다

두꺼운 modifies 이불 in the noun-modifier shape
Since it's winter, I took out my thick padded coat.
nuance: 두껍다 describes a FLAT thing being thick — a book, a blanket, a wall, a coat, a slice — and is the opposite of 얇다. It is ㅂ-IRREGULAR: 두껍다 → 두꺼워요 → 두꺼운 → 두꺼우니까 → 두꺼워서, so the regular-looking 두껍어요/두껍은 are the standard beginner errors. The contrast every English speaker needs is 두껍다 vs 굵다: both translate as 'thick,' but 두껍다 is for flat/layered objects (두꺼운 책) while 굵다 is for ROUND/cylindrical things — a thick rope, a thick tree trunk, thick noodles, or thick fingers are 굵다 (굵은 밧줄, 굵은 면), and using 두껍다 there sounds wrong. So 'thick legs' is 다리가 굵다, not 두껍다. The noun is 두께 ('thickness'), and the idiom 낯이 두껍다 / 얼굴이 두껍다 means 'shameless, thick-skinned.' Register is neutral.

adverb 얇게 + 썰다, a common cooking instruction
idiom — literally 'thin ears,' meaning you believe whatever you hear
